lesson_1.topicLabel: Enquiry 01: Mountains, Islands & Rival City-States (c. 800–500 BC)
lesson_1.title: Why Was Ancient Greece Split into Rival City-States, Yet United by Culture?
lesson_1.spokenTitle: Why was Ancient Greece split into rival city-states, yet united by culture?

cards.heading: Mountains, Islands & Poleis
cards.stat: 1,000+ Aegean Islands & Rival City-States
cards.connective: Why was Ancient Greece split into rival city-states, yet united by culture?
cards.html: Steep mountains and over a thousand Aegean islands kept Greek valleys apart. Instead of one king, towns like Athens and Sparta formed rival city-states with their own laws.
cards.spoken: Why was Ancient Greece split into rival city-states, yet united by culture? <short pause> Steep mountains and over a thousand Aegean islands kept Greek valleys apart. Instead of one king, towns like Athens and Sparta formed rival city-states with their own laws.

cards.heading: High Acropolis & Busy Agora
cards.stat: Fortified Hilltop Temples & Open Market
cards.connective: Even when city-states argued, almost every Greek town shared two key spaces.
cards.html: Families sheltered on a rocky walled hilltop called the Acropolis, crowned with marble temples. Below lay the sunny Agora marketplace, where traders sold figs and men debated city laws.
cards.spoken: Even when city-states argued, almost every Greek town shared two key spaces. <short pause> Families sheltered on a rocky walled hilltop called the Acropolis , crowned with marble temples. Below lay the sunny Agora marketplace , where traders sold figs and men debated city laws .

cards.heading: 24 Letters & Sea Trade
cards.stat: 24-Letter Alphabet, Olive Oil & Pottery
cards.connective: Across the sea, wooden trading ships carried goods and ideas together.
cards.html: Proud Greeks called themselves Hellenes and adapted Phoenician signs into a 24-letter alphabet with vowels. Merchant ships traded golden olive oil and painted pottery overseas for vital wheat grain.
cards.spoken: Across the sea, wooden trading ships carried goods and ideas together. <short pause> Proud Greeks called themselves Hellenes and adapted Phoenician signs into a 24-letter alphabet with vowels. Merchant ships traded golden olive oil and painted pottery overseas for vital wheat grain.

cards.heading: Rival Towns, One Greek Family
cards.stat: Shared Language, Gods & Alphabet Across Sea
cards.connective: Geography divided Greek valleys, yet sea routes bound their culture together.
cards.html: Rival poleis guarded their own walls, laws, and silver coins. Yet busy sea routes united Greeks through one shared language, one alphabet, and the Olympian gods.
cards.spoken: Geography divided Greek valleys, yet sea routes bound their culture together. <short pause> Rival poleis guarded their own walls, laws, and silver coins. Yet busy sea routes united Greeks through one shared language , one alphabet, and the Olympian gods .

lesson_1.takeaway: Steep mountains and Aegean islands split Greece into rival city-states, yet sea trade, a 24-letter alphabet, and shared gods united all Hellenes.
vocab: 1. Polis
An independent Greek city-state with its own laws and farmland.
2. Acropolis
The high walled hilltop of a city-state crowned with temples.
3. Agora
Open-air marketplace where citizens shopped and debated city laws.
lesson_1.provenanceNote: British Museum, Metropolitan Museum of Art, Louvre, Archaeological Museums of Greece & Wikimedia Commons (Zero AI Imagery)
lesson_1.spokenTakeaway: Here is the big story in one sentence. <short pause> Steep mountains and Aegean islands split Greece into rival city-states, yet sea trade, a 24-letter alphabet, and shared gods united all Hellenes.

lesson_2.topicLabel: Enquiry 02: Growing Up in Athens and Sparta (c. 508–430 BC)
lesson_2.title: How Different Was Daily Life in Democratic Athens and Warrior Sparta?
lesson_2.spokenTitle: How different was daily life in democratic Athens and warrior Sparta?

cards.heading: People-Power on the Pnyx
cards.stat: 500 Random Jurors & Ostrakon Shard Votes
cards.connective: How different was daily life in democratic Athens and warrior Sparta?
cards.html: Around 508 BC, male citizens in Athens invented direct democracy and voted on the rocky Pnyx hill. Yet women, enslaved people, and foreign metics were shut out from voting.
cards.spoken: How different was daily life in democratic Athens and warrior Sparta? <short pause> Around 508 BC, male citizens in Athens invented direct democracy and voted on the rocky Pnyx hill. Yet women, enslaved people, and foreign metics were shut out from voting.

cards.heading: Sparta's Tough Agoge Barracks
cards.stat: 2 Kings, Helot Farms & Age-7 Army Drills
cards.connective: Far inland beneath snowy mountains, warrior Sparta chose a very different path.
cards.html: Ruled by two kings, Sparta used conquered helot farmworkers so citizen men trained full-time for war. At age seven, barefoot boys entered harsh agoge barracks and slept on river reeds.
cards.spoken: Far inland beneath snowy mountains, warrior Sparta chose a very different path. <short pause> Ruled by two kings , Sparta used conquered helot farmworkers so citizen men trained full-time for war. At age seven, barefoot boys entered harsh agoge barracks and slept on river reeds.

cards.heading: Schoolrooms vs Outdoor Sport
cards.stat: Athenian Tutors vs Spartan Women Landowners
cards.connective: Childhood for boys and girls looked completely different in the two cities.
cards.html: Wealthy Athenian boys studied reading, music, and poetry while girls learned weaving indoors. Meanwhile, Spartan girls wrestled and threw javelins outdoors, and Spartan women owned land themselves.
cards.spoken: Childhood for boys and girls looked completely different in the two cities. <short pause> Wealthy Athenian boys studied reading, music, and poetry while girls learned weaving indoors. Meanwhile, Spartan girls wrestled and threw javelins outdoors, and Spartan women owned land themselves.

cards.heading: Votes & Art vs Army Order
cards.stat: Sea-Trading Democracy vs Land Army Power
cards.connective: Athens and Sparta proved two Greek cities could live in opposite ways.
cards.html: Sea-trading Athens prized citizen debates, silver coins, and marble art, though women lacked rights. Landlocked Sparta rejected luxury for strict army discipline, yet gave women far greater freedom.
cards.spoken: Athens and Sparta proved two Greek cities could live in opposite ways. <short pause> Sea-trading Athens prized citizen debates , silver coins, and marble art, though women lacked rights. Landlocked Sparta rejected luxury for strict army discipline , yet gave women far greater freedom .

lesson_2.takeaway: Sea-trading Athens invented citizen democracy and prized arts, while warrior Sparta trained boys in agoge barracks from age seven and gave women greater freedom.
vocab: 1. Democracy
Rule by the people, where male Athenian citizens voted on laws.
2. Ostrakon
Broken pottery shard scratched with a name to banish a leader.
3. Agoge
Sparta's tough army training barracks entered by boys at age seven.
lesson_2.provenanceNote: British Museum, Metropolitan Museum of Art, Louvre, Archaeological Museums of Greece & Wikimedia Commons (Zero AI Imagery)
lesson_2.spokenTakeaway: Here is the big story in one sentence. <short pause> Sea-trading Athens invented citizen democracy and prized arts, while warrior Sparta trained boys in agoge barracks from age seven and gave women greater freedom.

lesson_3.topicLabel: Enquiry 03: Mount Olympus, Myths & The Ancient Olympics (776–400 BC)
lesson_3.title: How Did Greek Gods Inspire Temples, Myths, and the Olympic Games?
lesson_3.spokenTitle: How did Greek gods inspire temples, myths, and the Olympic Games?

cards.heading: Mount Olympus & Marble Temples
cards.stat: 12 Olympian Gods & Athens's Marble Parthenon
cards.connective: How did Greek gods inspire temples, myths, and the Olympic Games?
cards.html: Greeks believed twelve gods ruled from snowy Mount Olympus, led by thunder-hurling Zeus. Cities built gleaming temples like Athens's Parthenon and roasted offerings at outdoor altars.
cards.spoken: How did Greek gods inspire temples, myths, and the Olympic Games? <short pause> Greeks believed twelve gods ruled from snowy Mount Olympus , led by thunder-hurling Zeus . Cities built gleaming temples like Athens's Parthenon and roasted offerings at outdoor altars.

cards.heading: Delphi's Oracle & Vase Myths
cards.stat: Apollo's Priestess & Painted Clay Story Jars
cards.connective: Leaders and families also looked to sacred shrines and exciting hero tales.
cards.html: Before wars, generals climbed mountain Delphi to hear riddles from Apollo's Oracle. Potters also painted brave heroes like Heracles and Odysseus onto glossy black-figure and red-figure vases.
cards.spoken: Leaders and families also looked to sacred shrines and exciting hero tales. <short pause> Before wars, generals climbed mountain Delphi to hear riddles from Apollo's Oracle . Potters also painted brave heroes like Heracles and Odysseus onto glossy black-figure and red-figure vases.

cards.heading: 776 BC: Games at Olympia
cards.stat: Sacred Truce, Chariots & Wild-Olive Crowns
cards.connective: Every four summers, honouring Zeus brought rival cities together in peace.
cards.html: From 776 BC, a Sacred Truce paused wars so athletes travelled safely to Olympia. Barefoot runners, wrestlers, and charioteers competed for a sacred wild-olive kotinos crown.
cards.spoken: Every four summers, honouring Zeus brought rival cities together in peace. <short pause> From 776 BC , a Sacred Truce paused wars so athletes travelled safely to Olympia. Barefoot runners, wrestlers, and charioteers competed for a sacred wild-olive kotinos crown .

cards.heading: Faith Uniting Rival Greeks
cards.stat: One Stadium Track & Shared Hero Stories
cards.connective: Temples, painted jars, and stadium races wove Greek life into one story.
cards.html: Worshipping the twelve Olympians filled Greece with marble temples and painted myth vases. Every four years at Olympia's running track, warring city-states cheered side by side.
cards.spoken: Temples, painted jars, and stadium races wove Greek life into one story. <short pause> Worshipping the twelve Olympians filled Greece with marble temples and painted myth vases . Every four years at Olympia's running track , warring city-states cheered side by side.

lesson_3.takeaway: Belief in the twelve Olympian gods inspired marble temples like the Parthenon, hero myths on painted vases, and peaceful Olympic Games from 776 BC.
vocab: 1. Parthenon
White-marble temple high on Athens's Acropolis honouring Athena.
2. Oracle
Sacred shrine at Delphi where a priestess spoke advice from Apollo.
3. Sacred Truce
Peace deal pausing Greek wars during the Ancient Olympic Games.
lesson_3.provenanceNote: British Museum, Metropolitan Museum of Art, Louvre, Archaeological Museums of Greece & Wikimedia Commons (Zero AI Imagery)
lesson_3.spokenTakeaway: Here is the big story in one sentence. <short pause> Belief in the twelve Olympian gods inspired marble temples like the Parthenon, hero myths on painted vases, and peaceful Olympic Games from 776 BC.

lesson_4.title: How Did Tiny Greek City-States Defeat the Giant Persian Empire?
lesson_4.spokenTitle: How did tiny Greek city-states defeat the giant Persian Empire?

cards.heading: 490 BC: Phalanx at Marathon
cards.stat: Shield-Wall Charge & 26-Mile Victory Run
cards.connective: How did tiny Greek city-states defeat the giant Persian Empire?
cards.html: In 490 BC, King Darius's Persian army landed at Marathon to punish Athens. Charging citizen hoplites locked bronze shields in a tight phalanx and smashed the invaders.
cards.spoken: How did tiny Greek city-states defeat the giant Persian Empire? <short pause> In 490 BC , King Darius's Persian army landed at Marathon to punish Athens. Charging citizen hoplites locked bronze shields in a tight phalanx and smashed the invaders.

cards.heading: 480 BC: Stand at Thermopylae
cards.stat: 300 Spartans Hold Narrow Pass for 3 Days
cards.connective: Ten years later, Darius's son King Xerxes led an even bigger invasion.
cards.html: Spartan King Leonidas and 300 Spartans guarded the narrow coastal pass of Thermopylae for three days. When a traitor showed Xerxes a mountain path, Leonidas fought on so allies escaped.
cards.spoken: Ten years later, Darius's son King Xerxes led an even bigger invasion. <short pause> Spartan King Leonidas and 300 Spartans guarded the narrow coastal pass of Thermopylae for three days. When a traitor showed Xerxes a mountain path, Leonidas fought on so allies escaped.

cards.heading: Triremes Win at Salamis
cards.stat: 170 Oarsmen & Bronze Rams in Narrow Strait
cards.connective: At sea, clever Admiral Themistocles set a trap in narrow waters.
cards.html: Themistocles lured Persia's huge fleet into the tight Strait of Salamis. Powered by 170 rowers, nimble Greek triremes rammed the crowded Persian ships and won.
cards.spoken: At sea, clever Admiral Themistocles set a trap in narrow waters. <short pause> Themistocles lured Persia's huge fleet into the tight Strait of Salamis . Powered by 170 rowers, nimble Greek triremes rammed the crowded Persian ships and won.

cards.heading: United City-States Stay Free
cards.stat: Teamwork, Smart Tactics & Local Geography
cards.connective: Teamwork and smart tactics defeated the largest empire in the ancient world.
cards.html: Using hoplite shield-walls, narrow mountain passes, and fast wooden triremes, united Greeks beat Persia by 479 BC. Keeping their freedom sparked Athens's Golden Age.
cards.spoken: Teamwork and smart tactics defeated the largest empire in the ancient world. <short pause> Using hoplite shield-walls , narrow mountain passes, and fast wooden triremes , united Greeks beat Persia by 479 BC. Keeping their freedom sparked Athens's Golden Age.

lesson_4.takeaway: By uniting together and using hoplite shield-walls, narrow passes, and fast trireme warships, tiny Greek city-states defeated mighty Persia between 490 and 479 BC.
vocab: 1. Hoplite
Heavily armed Greek citizen-soldier with bronze shield and spear.
2. Phalanx
Tight shoulder-to-shoulder block of hoplites locking shields.
3. Trireme
Fast Greek warship rowed by 170 oarsmen with a bronze ram.
lesson_4.provenanceNote: British Museum, Metropolitan Museum of Art, Louvre, Archaeological Museums of Greece & Wikimedia Commons (Zero AI Imagery)
lesson_4.spokenTakeaway: Here is the big story in one sentence. <short pause> By uniting together and using hoplite shield-walls, narrow passes, and fast trireme warships, tiny Greek city-states defeated mighty Persia between 490 and 479 BC.

lesson_5.topicLabel: Enquiry 05: Greek Theatre, Philosophy, Maths & Medicine (c. 460–322 BC)
lesson_5.title: How Did Greek Thinkers, Doctors, and Writers Change Human Knowledge?
lesson_5.spokenTitle: How did Greek thinkers, doctors, and writers change human knowledge?

cards.heading: Hillside Theatres & Masks
cards.stat: 14,000 Seats at Epidaurus for Greek Plays
cards.connective: How did Greek thinkers, doctors, and writers change human knowledge?
cards.html: Carved into sunny hillsides like Epidaurus, stone amphitheatres seated 14,000 spectators with clear acoustics. Masked actors performed sad tragedies and funny comedies for rich and poor citizens.
cards.spoken: How did Greek thinkers, doctors, and writers change human knowledge? <short pause> Carved into sunny hillsides like Epidaurus , stone amphitheatres seated 14,000 spectators with clear acoustics. Masked actors performed sad tragedies and funny comedies for rich and poor citizens.

cards.heading: Socrates, Plato & Aristotle
cards.stat: Questioning Beliefs & Sorting Nature's Facts
cards.connective: In Athens, philosophers — meaning lovers of wisdom — asked bold new questions.
cards.html: Barefoot Socrates questioned citizens in the Agora, while Plato opened his Academy school. Next, Aristotle observed and sorted hundreds of plants and animals to build science.
cards.spoken: In Athens, philosophers — meaning lovers of wisdom — asked bold new questions. <short pause> Barefoot Socrates questioned citizens in the Agora, while Plato opened his Academy school. Next, Aristotle observed and sorted hundreds of plants and animals to build science.

cards.heading: Hippocrates, Geometry & Eureka
cards.stat: Bedside Notes, Triangles & Clever Levers
cards.connective: Doctors and mathematicians also looked for natural rules instead of magic.
cards.html: On Kos, doctor Hippocrates checked natural symptoms and wrote the ethical Hippocratic Oath. Meanwhile, Pythagoras and Euclid mastered geometry, and Archimedes shouted "Eureka!" over water puzzles.
cards.spoken: Doctors and mathematicians also looked for natural rules instead of magic. <short pause> On Kos, doctor Hippocrates checked natural symptoms and wrote the ethical Hippocratic Oath . Meanwhile, Pythagoras and Euclid mastered geometry, and Archimedes shouted "Eureka!" over water puzzles.

cards.heading: Testing Ideas Through Reason
cards.stat: Roots of Modern Drama, Medicine & Maths
cards.connective: Together, Greek writers and scientists changed how humans study the world.
cards.html: Instead of blaming everything on angry gods, Greeks used careful observation, geometry, and open debate. Their plays, medical notes, and maths still guide modern classrooms.
cards.spoken: Together, Greek writers and scientists changed how humans study the world. <short pause> Instead of blaming everything on angry gods, Greeks used careful observation , geometry , and open debate. Their plays, medical notes, and maths still guide modern classrooms .

lesson_5.takeaway: Greek playwrights, philosophers like Socrates and Aristotle, doctor Hippocrates, and mathematicians like Euclid taught people to question, observe nature, and prove ideas.
vocab: 1. Amphitheatre
Open-air stone theatre with curved rows carved into a hillside.
2. Philosopher
A 'lover of wisdom' who searches for truth through questions.
3. Geometry
Branch of mathematics studying lines, angles, and shapes.
lesson_5.provenanceNote: British Museum, Metropolitan Museum of Art, Louvre, Archaeological Museums of Greece & Wikimedia Commons (Zero AI Imagery)
lesson_5.spokenTakeaway: Here is the big story in one sentence. <short pause> Greek playwrights, philosophers like Socrates and Aristotle, doctor Hippocrates, and mathematicians like Euclid taught people to question, observe nature, and prove ideas.

lesson_6.topicLabel: Enquiry 06: Alexander the Great & Greece’s Legacy Today (336–146 BC)
lesson_6.title: How Did Alexander Spread Greek Ideas That Still Shape Our World Today?
lesson_6.spokenTitle: How did Alexander spread Greek ideas that still shape our world today?

cards.heading: Alexander & Vast Conquests
cards.stat: 11 Unbeaten Years Across Egypt to India
cards.connective: How did Alexander spread Greek ideas that still shape our world today?
cards.html: Taught by Aristotle and riding wild Bucephalus, young Alexander the Great marched from Macedon to India. Founding new cities blended Greek and eastern ways into Hellenistic culture.
cards.spoken: How did Alexander spread Greek ideas that still shape our world today? <short pause> Taught by Aristotle and riding wild Bucephalus , young Alexander the Great marched from Macedon to India. Founding new cities blended Greek and eastern ways into Hellenistic culture .

cards.heading: Alexandria's Library & Rome
cards.stat: Hundreds of Thousands of Scrolls & 146 BC
cards.connective: In Egypt, port Alexandria became a beacon of Greek science and books.
cards.html: Scholars studied stars and geometry inside Alexandria's Great Library beside the tall Pharos Lighthouse. Even after Roman legions conquered Greece in 146 BC, Romans copied Greek art and books.
cards.spoken: In Egypt, port Alexandria became a beacon of Greek science and books. <short pause> Scholars studied stars and geometry inside Alexandria's Great Library beside the tall Pharos Lighthouse . Even after Roman legions conquered Greece in 146 BC, Romans copied Greek art and books.

cards.heading: Votes, Words & 1896 Olympics
cards.stat: 14 Nations Revive Modern Olympics in Athens
cards.connective: More than two thousand years later, Greek gifts still surround us every day.
cards.html: Elections, juries, stone columns, and words like school, planet, and history come from Greece. In 1896, fourteen nations launched the Modern Olympic Games inside Athens's marble stadium.
cards.spoken: More than two thousand years later, Greek gifts still surround us every day. <short pause> Elections, juries, stone columns , and words like school , planet , and history come from Greece. In 1896 , fourteen nations launched the Modern Olympic Games inside Athens's marble stadium.

cards.heading: Greek Ideas Across the World
cards.stat: Democracy, Science, Architecture & Sport
cards.connective: Conquests, libraries, and Roman admirers carried Greek ideas across centuries.
cards.html: From Alexandria's scrolls to modern town halls and sports tracks, Ancient Greece left a lasting legacy. Its curiosity still shapes democracy, language, and science worldwide.
cards.spoken: Conquests, libraries, and Roman admirers carried Greek ideas across centuries. <short pause> From Alexandria's scrolls to modern town halls and sports tracks, Ancient Greece left a lasting legacy . Its curiosity still shapes democracy, language, and science worldwide.

lesson_6.takeaway: Alexander the Great and Alexandria's Great Library spread Greek learning afar, leaving a lasting legacy in our democracy, language, buildings, and Olympic Games.
vocab: 1. Hellenistic
Blended culture mixing Greek language and art with eastern ideas.
2. Alexandria
Egyptian port famed for the Pharos Lighthouse and Great Library.
3. Legacy
Ideas, words, and traditions handed down that shape life today.
lesson_6.provenanceNote: British Museum, Metropolitan Museum of Art, Louvre, Archaeological Museums of Greece & Wikimedia Commons (Zero AI Imagery)
lesson_6.spokenTakeaway: Here is the big story in one sentence. <short pause> Alexander the Great and Alexandria's Great Library spread Greek learning afar, leaving a lasting legacy in our democracy, language, buildings, and Olympic Games.
